Needs to have its own type system. ⁓ That type system is going to represent the data coming in and the data leaving that API. That's what's important here. This is why no common type system, because every package creates a firewall in and of itself to any other package in the system. So the type system belongs to a package. Now, when it comes to this idea of data flowing in and out of a package API, you have a couple of choices.

We can work with concrete types, or we can work with interface types. Now, ideally, we want to start with concrete types. We call these concrete types, like the keyword struct allows us to find a concrete type, because that is real data. That's the data that's actually being stored, actually being transformed, actually being moved around the program. And when we build an API that uses a concrete type, what we're saying is that this API accepts data based on what it is.

It is this one thing. It's a user, it's a product, it's a widget, it's something. It's based on what it is. ⁓ And that same data can be returned based on what it is. Now, a concrete, say function, a function that takes just concrete data, you could almost argue that it's limited because it can only work with that data and only that kind of data. And there are times where we want to write functions that need to be flexible to work with not just one kind of data.

And this is where our interface types come in. Our interface types allow us to write functions that accept data not based on what it is, but based on what it can do.
